planting.note: Plant rooted divisions or plugs in spring into acidic, sandy, well-drained soil; Augusta is one of the original Kentville Research Station lowbush releases and fills in as a low rhizomatous mat rather than an upright bush.

directions: Augusta is a midseason lowbush blueberry released from Nova Scotia's Kentville Research Station, selected from a native stand for large, attractive berries that weigh noticeably more than the typical wild clone. Like other lowbush selections it spreads by underground rhizomes into a dense low colony and is managed on a two-year burn-or-mow cycle, with one year's growth sacrificed to renew the wood that carries the following season's bloom and crop. Grow it in full sun on lean, acidic, well-drained soil, since richer garden loam favors leafy growth over fruit set. Its reliable midseason ripening and fruit size have made it a parent of later Kentville introductions, including 'Fundy'.

planting.note: Plant rooted divisions or plugs in spring into acidic, sandy, well-drained soil; Brunswick was selected from a commercial wild stand in Albert County, New Brunswick and, like other named lowbush clones, performs best paired with a second cultivar for cross-pollination.

directions: Brunswick was selected in 1965 from a native lowbush stand in Albert County, New Brunswick, and became the second named clone released from the Kentville Research Station lowbush blueberry program. It stays low and dense even for a lowbush selection, knitting into a tight rhizomatous groundcover rarely more than a foot tall, with glossy dark green leaves that turn crimson and burgundy in fall. Berries are intensely sweet with a distinctive wine-like flavor and are borne heavily late in the season, usually ripening through July. As with other lowbush clones, manage it on a biennial mow-or-burn renewal cycle and expect better fruit set when a second lowbush cultivar is planted nearby.

planting.note: Plant rooted divisions or plugs in spring into acidic, sandy, well-drained soil; Cumberland is self-incompatible, so interplant with another named lowbush clone such as 'Fundy' or 'Blomidon' to ensure a full crop.

directions: Cumberland was selected in 1964 from a native stand in Cumberland County, Nova Scotia, and ranked among the strongest performers in Kentville Research Station field trials of wild lowbush clones. Its globose, lightly bloomed berries are large for the species and carry a notably high percentage of soluble solids once ripe, giving them a sweeter profile than many lowbush selections even though the fruit is somewhat softer and less firm. Because Cumberland is self-incompatible, plant it alongside a second lowbush cultivar for reliable pollination and fruit set. Like other named lowbush clones it spreads into a low rhizomatous colony and is renewed on a two-year mow-or-burn cycle rather than pruned as an upright shrub.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in very acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in full sun; St. Cloud is a University of Minnesota half-high release best planted with Northblue, Northcountry, or Northsky for cross-pollination.

directions: St. Cloud is a University of Minnesota half-high blueberry bred for the extreme cold hardiness of lowbush parentage combined with the larger, more upright habit of highbush types. It ripens early to midseason, comparable to 'Northblue', producing medium-to-large, firm, dark blue berries with good fresh flavor that hold up well for fresh eating, U-pick, and freezing. Established plants typically bear around seven pounds of fruit per bush once mature. Because it is an interspecific hybrid, cross-pollination with a second compatible cultivar such as 'Northblue', 'Northcountry', or 'Northsky' improves both berry size and total yield.
sources: University of Minnesota Extension — Half-High Blueberries for Minnesota

planting.note: Plant a bare-root or container tree in spring in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Flanders Giant, also sold as Large Dutch medlar, is self-fertile and needs no second tree to set a full crop.

directions: Flanders Giant, also traded as Large Dutch medlar, is an RHS-recommended selection grown for russet-brown fruit that reaches roughly three inches across and yields noticeably more usable flesh than an ordinary seedling medlar. Flowers open as large white cups in late spring on a small, spreading, picturesque tree, followed by fruit that ripens outwardly from October into early November but remains hard and astringent until it bletts. Store the picked fruit in a cool spot for several weeks after the first frosts until it softens, darkens, and develops the rich, wine-spiced flavor typical of bletted medlar, then eat it fresh or cook it into jelly or paste. The tree tolerates a wide range of soils, including chalk and clay, and needs only light pruning to remove dead or crossing wood.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society — Mespilus germanica 'Flanders Giant'
